items.finding: Non-native fish suppression flows with daily fluctuations between 142 and 566 m3/s were released from Glen Canyon Dam each January through March from 2003 to 2005, representing a special-event departure from the standard MLFF/LTEMP flow regime implemented for a specific ecological management objective.

items.finding: A series of pulsed flows released from Glen Canyon Dam in 1965 to lower the tailwater bed scoured the channel of sand; because tributary sand supply to Glen Canyon itself is negligible, the riverbed there is now armored with cobbles and the resulting channel bed degradation is irreversible under the current flow and sediment supply regime.

items.finding: The 1996 HFE, a 7-day sustained release of 1,274 m3/s beginning March 26, was the first controlled flood used to comprehensively test whether high releases from Glen Canyon Dam could redistribute sand from the riverbed to channel margins; because it followed two years of below-average tributary sand input, suspended sediment progressively coarsened and depleted during the event.

items.finding: The November 3, 1997 Test Flow (a constant 872 m3/s release for 48 hours), the first Reclamation attempt at a post-tributary-flood sediment-redistribution release, did not significantly aggrade sandbars because its magnitude was insufficient to distribute sand to open depositional locations at higher elevations.
items.source_location: extracted text; 1997 Test Flow section

items.finding: The 2000 Low Summer Steady Flow Experiment (4-day 864 m3/s release, 3 months of constant 227 m3/s, then a 4-day 881 m3/s release) produced minimal sandbar building because the Paria River had supplied very little sediment beforehand, and the sustained low, steady discharge instead allowed proliferation of invasive tamarisk seedlings on bare sand deposits.
items.source_location: extracted text; The 2000 Low Summer Steady Flow Experiment section

items.finding: During 2004-2020, a period that included seven controlled floods (HFEs), a median Glen Canyon Dam discharge of 350 m3/s, and above-average tributary sand input in more than half the years, net sandbar deposition occurred at 86 percent of long-term monitoring sites, in contrast to the preceding 1990-2003 period when only one controlled flood exceeded the nominal powerplant capacity of 940 m3/s.
items.source_location: extracted text; Abstract

items.finding: At wide reattachment bars and upper pool deposits, vegetation stabilization and vertical aggradation during successive HFEs have progressively narrowed the channel and reduced the accommodation space available for further deposition, so that at these sites HFEs can at best only replace sediment eroded during normal dam operations between events rather than produce net growth.
items.source_location: extracted text; Discussion, Sandbar Response to the High-Flow Experiment Protocol section

items.finding: Separation bars and undifferentiated eddy bars have not been effectively rebuilt by the HFE protocol and have continued to gradually decrease in volume over time, because although they consistently aggrade during individual HFEs, the subsequent erosion at these unvegetated, wind-exposed sites is rapid.
items.source_location: extracted text; Discussion, Sandbar Response to the High-Flow Experiment Protocol section

items.finding: The sandbar monitoring dataset comprises ~1,800 repeat topographic/bathymetric surveys made annually or more frequently at 45 long-term study sites, which together represent only 7 to 9 percent of all sandbars in Marble and Grand Canyons respectively, yet were shown by comparison with larger samples to provide a consistent characterization of average sandbar response system-wide.
items.source_location: extracted text; Abstract

items.finding: The Lake Powell water quality model evolved from an original LARM hydrodynamic model (1973-74, 1979-80) to a BETTER model (1992-93 simulation, including DO), then was converted to CE-QUAL-W2 version 2.0 in 2001, and updated to version 3.2 in 2004 with the simulation period extended to 1990-2005; this version 3.2, 1990-2005 model is the one used in this study.

items.finding: In fall 2005 a plume of oxygen-depleted water in Lake Powell was captured in the penstock withdrawal zone and exported through Glen Canyon Dam, dropping tailwater dissolved oxygen below 4.0 mg/L in September 2005, violating EPA cold-water fishery DO criteria (1-day mean minimum 4.0 mg/L, 7-day mean minimum 5.0 mg/L, 30-day mean 6.5 mg/L).
items.source_location: extracted text; Section 1.1.4 Fall 2005 Oxygen Depletion

items.finding: Following the 2005 oxygen depletion event, Reclamation conducted turbine aeration tests that found operating Glen Canyon Dam turbines at lower flows and lower generating efficiencies increased aeration most; as a result, more turbines were run at lower flows during September-October 2005 to raise tailwater dissolved oxygen concentrations.
items.source_location: extracted text; Section 1.1.4 Fall 2005 Oxygen Depletion, Solutions

items.finding: Lake Powell's hydraulic retention time is about 2 years, based on an active reservoir capacity of roughly 24 million acre-feet and an average annual inflow of about 11 million acre-feet; year-to-year retention time has historically ranged between about 1 and 5 years.
items.source_location: extracted text; Section 4.3.1 Hydrology

items.finding: Lake Powell develops thermal stratification into epilimnion, metalimnion, and hypolimnion layers each year, beginning in spring and typically stable by July, persisting until autumn air temperatures drop and surface cooling drives vertical mixing back toward isothermal conditions.
items.source_location: extracted text; Section 4.3.3 Stratification

items.finding: Lake Powell exhibits three types of inflow-driven density currents - overflow (spring, warmer/lower-TDS inflow moving across the surface), underflow (winter, colder/higher-TDS inflow moving along the bottom), and interflow (summer/fall, inflow density intermediate between epilimnion and hypolimnion) - each transporting water and dissolved oxygen to different depths.
items.source_location: extracted text; Section 4.3.4 Density Currents

items.finding: In most years the metalimnetic oxygen minimum does not affect dam discharges because it sits well above the penstock elevation (3,470 ft), but in 2005 reservoir elevations were the lowest since initial filling and the low-DO metalimnetic water was located just above the penstock elevation, allowing oxygen-depleted water to pass through the dam.
items.source_location: extracted text; Section 4.4.4 Metalimnetic Minimum

items.finding: Of four CE-QUAL-W2 dissolved-oxygen simulation approaches tested at the Wahweap monitoring site over 1991-2005, the empirical CBOD (carbonaceous biochemical oxygen demand) loading method produced the lowest average mean error (AME 1.15), outperforming nutrient-plankton simulation (AME 3.04), zero-order sediment oxygen demand (AME 1.91), and measured inflow BOD (AME 1.38).

items.finding: The empirical CBOD equations were calibrated only for the 1990-2005 period and for the specific reservoir elevations and flow rates experienced during that period, so they may not be valid for future simulations or for elevations and flows outside that historical range.

items.finding: The calibrated Lake Powell CE-QUAL-W2 model is recommended for use in setting the measurement frequency and location of the reservoir water-quality monitoring program, and for evaluating proposed dam modifications, such as the temperature control device, by simulating them over a historical period and comparing modeled to observed results.

items.finding: The 19 LTEMP long-term strategies produced unavoidable tradeoffs across performance metrics, with no strategy dominating all others; depending on which stakeholder weights were applied, three alternatives (B, D, and G) were top-ranked, with Alternative B favored by hydropower-focused stakeholders, G by those valuing natural-process restoration, and D by the remaining stakeholders.

items.finding: The Assistant Secretary of the Interior invited 27 Federal, State, tribal, and nongovernmental agencies to participate in a swing-weighting exercise expressing relative value on LTEMP resource goals and performance metrics; only 14 of the 27 invited agencies, including the two joint-lead agencies (Reclamation and NPS), chose to participate.

items.finding: Two primary decision-analysis methods -- multicriteria decision analysis (MCDA, using the Simple Multi-Attribute Rating Technique with swing weighting) and expected value of information (EVPI/EVXI) -- were used to evaluate the 19 long-term strategies against 18 performance metrics and to determine how much uncertainty mattered to the ranking of alternatives.
items.source_location: extracted text; Abstract

items.finding: The joint-lead agencies determined that two decades of GCDAMP research since the 1996 Record of Decision provided enough knowledge to shift LTEMP from the original Resilience-Experimentalist (RE) adaptive-management approach toward a Decision-Theoretic (DT) approach, explicitly articulating uncertainty as competing hypotheses linked to future management actions.
items.source_location: extracted text; section 3.3.1 Adaptive Management Versus Experimental Management

items.finding: LTEMP alternatives distinguish state-dependent triggers (conditions of system state, such as the 2007 interim guidelines' annual release volume, that switch management actions in recognition of natural variation) from information-dependent triggers (indications that the state of scientific knowledge has changed enough to warrant a new management approach, such as evidence on whether trout management flows are effective).
items.source_location: extracted text; section 3.3.3 Deconstructing Complex Alternatives

items.finding: The expected value of perfect information (EVPI) was used to set an upper bound on the value of experimental or adaptive management by comparing expected performance under uncertainty to expected performance if uncertainty could be fully resolved before a decision; the related expected value of partial information (EVXI) evaluates the value of resolving only part of the uncertainty (e.g., a single hydrological or sediment trace).
items.source_location: extracted text; section 3.3.4 Value of Information

items.finding: The decision analysis used 18 quantitative performance metrics tied to 8 of 12 fundamental resource goals, spanning minimum adult humpback chub (3,000-8,500 fish), rainbow trout catch rate (1.0-5.0 fish/angler-hour), hydropower generation value ($120-200 million/year), hydropower capacity value ($10-50 million/year), and sand load index (0-0.6), each with a defined desired direction and range used in stakeholder swing-weighting.
items.source_location: extracted text; table 1, Summary of the 18 performance metrics used in the decision analysis

items.finding: Across the seven LTEMP alternatives, minimum base-operation flow ranged from 5,000 to 8,000 ft3/s while maximum flow was uniformly 25,000 ft3/s for all alternatives; the allowed daily range varied from 0 to 12,000 ft3/s, and ramp rates were fixed at 4,000 ft3/s per hour for increasing flow but ranged from 1,500 to 4,000 ft3/s per hour for decreasing flow.
items.source_location: extracted text; section 5.1.1 Monthly Release Pattern and Other Base Operations

items.finding: High-flow experimental releases (HFEs) exceed the operational maximum daily flow and can reach as high as 45,000 ft3/s depending on available generation units; under the 2011 HFE protocol most HFEs are capped at a 96-hour maximum duration, but some LTEMP alternatives allow extended-duration HFEs when adequate sediment supply is available.
items.source_location: extracted text; section 5.1.2 High-Flow Experiments

items.finding: Trout management flows (TMFs) -- an experimental release pattern of roughly 20,000 ft3/s for 2-7 days followed by a rapid drop to 5,000-8,000 ft3/s -- are designed to strand young-of-year rainbow trout, trading rainbow trout fishery quality against reduced downstream emigration risk to humpback chub; TMFs had never been implemented at Glen Canyon Dam as of this report.
